Because we are NYDFS-licensed and provide consumer credit, the security roadmap should be driven primarily by **23 NYCRR Part 500**, with the FTC Safeguards and Red Flags Rules as federal overlays. All transition periods for the amended Part 500 have now expired, so these are current obligations—not future targets. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity))

## Recommended priorities

1. **Part 500 gap assessment and evidence programme**
   - Confirm whether we are a standard, limited-exemption or **Class A** entity.
   - Map every requirement to a control owner, evidence source and remediation date.
   - The next filing is due **April 15, 2027**, covering calendar year 2026, and must be signed by the highest-ranking executive and CISO. Supporting evidence and remediation records must be retained for five years. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

2. **Identity and privileged access**
   - MFA for every individual accessing our systems, subject only to formally approved equivalent controls.
   - Least privilege, restricted privileged-account use, prompt leaver termination and at least annual access reviews.
   - DFS’s May 21, 2026 guidance particularly emphasises phishing-resistant MFA, secure MFA enrolment and privileged-access reviews. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

3. **Asset, data and encryption hygiene**
   - Maintain a complete, accurate system inventory covering ownership, location, sensitivity, support expiry and recovery objectives.
   - Encrypt non-public/customer information in transit and at rest.
   - Implement defensible retention and secure-disposal processes. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

4. **Vulnerability management and secure engineering**
   - Conduct internal and external penetration testing at least annually.
   - Run risk-based automated vulnerability scanning and scan promptly after material changes.
   - Maintain secure-development standards and security assessment of third-party applications.
   - Under the FTC rule, continuous monitoring—or annual penetration testing plus vulnerability assessments at least every six months—is required for covered institutions above the relevant exemption threshold. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

5. **Operational resilience and incident readiness**
   - Annually test incident response, BCDR and actual restoration of critical systems from protected backups.
   - Build notification decision trees into the playbooks:
     - NYDFS cybersecurity incident: no later than **72 hours** after determination.
     - NYDFS extortion payment: **24 hours**, followed by a written explanation within 30 days.
     - FTC event involving at least 500 consumers’ unencrypted customer information: no later than **30 days after discovery**. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

6. **Third-party and cloud risk**
   - Tier providers, perform pre-contract due diligence and periodically reassess them.
   - Ensure contracts address access controls/MFA, encryption, rapid event notification and cybersecurity commitments.
   - Include critical providers in incident and continuity exercises, with tested exit and access-revocation procedures. DFS issued detailed guidance on this in October 2025. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry-guidance/industry-letters/il20251021-guidance-managing-risks-third-party))

7. **Governance and identity-theft controls**
   - Complete and document an annual risk assessment; obtain annual approval of cybersecurity policies; provide written CISO reporting to the governing body.
   - Maintain the federally required written **Identity Theft Prevention/Red Flags programme** for covered consumer accounts, including periodic updates, service-provider oversight and annual reporting to the board or senior management. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

### If we meet the Class A thresholds

Class A companies have additional mandatory work: independent cybersecurity audits, privileged-access management, common-password blocking, endpoint detection and response, and centralised logging/security alerting. The threshold generally requires at least $20 million in relevant annual revenue plus either more than 2,000 employees or more than $1 billion in annual group revenue, subject to the regulation’s affiliate rules. ([dfs.ny.gov](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/23_nycrr_part_500))

**Planning recommendation:** make the annual risk assessment and Part 500 evidence review the first-quarter activity, then fund IAM/PAM, asset and data inventory, resilience testing, vulnerability management and third-party assurance based on the identified gaps. We also need the list of other lending states to add their breach-notification and state-specific privacy/security requirements; those cannot be assessed reliably from the New York licence alone.

### What the redesigned flow should include

1. **Layered, just-in-time explanations**
   - On each collection screen, briefly explain **what data is requested, why, whether it is required, and the immediate consequence of providing or withholding it**.
   - Link to a complete notice covering the controller/DPO, purposes and legal bases, recipients, transfers, retention, rights, complaints, and automated decision-making.
   - Keep information concise, visible before collection, and easily accessible later. See [EDPB Guidelines on transparency under Regulation 2016/679](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/transparency_en) and [AEPD report on adapting online privacy policies to GDPR](https://www.aepd.es/prensa-y-comunicacion/notas-de-prensa/la-aepd-publica-los-resultados-de-su-informe-sobre-la).

2. **A genuinely child-friendly version**
   - Because children meaningfully use the app, use short sentences, concrete examples, age-appropriate illustrations, and explanations of consequences—not legal jargon.
   - Test comprehension with children in the relevant age groups. The EDPB specifically requires clear and plain language, especially when information is addressed to children: [Transparency Guidelines](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/transparency_en).

3. **Separate information from consent**
   - Do not make “I agree to the privacy policy” the basis for all processing.
   - Where consent is actually your lawful basis, request it separately for distinct optional purposes—such as analytics, personalised advertising, or optional personalisation—and record the user’s choice.
   - Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and must not be bundled into non-negotiable terms: [EDPB Guidelines 05/2020 on consent](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-052020-consent-under-regulation-2016679_en).

4. **No manipulative choice architecture**
   - Avoid preselected optional processing, prominent “Accept” buttons paired with hidden refusal paths, repeated nagging, confusing toggles, or suggesting the app cannot work when only optional tracking is refused.
   - Default to processing only data necessary for the service. See [AEPD: Dark patterns—Manipulation in Internet services](https://www.aepd.es/en/prensa-y-comunicacion/blog/dark-patterns-manipulation-in-internet-services).

5. **Gate trackers and SDKs correctly**
   - Inventory every SDK and anything that accesses or stores information on the device, including advertising IDs, pixels, fingerprinting, analytics and attribution tools.
   - Do not activate non-essential tracking until the necessary consent has been obtained. The ePrivacy rule is technology-neutral and extends beyond cookies: [EDPB Guidelines 2/2023 on Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-22023-technical-scope-art-53-eprivacy-directive_en).

6. **Design age assurance proportionately**
   - Decide which experiences actually require knowing whether somebody is a child. Avoid collecting an exact date of birth or identity document when an age-band or threshold result is enough.
   - Assess effectiveness, accessibility, data minimisation and the need for a DPIA. See [EDPB Statement 1/2025 on Age Assurance](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/topic/children_en).
   - Do not assume one parental-consent age works throughout the EU; obtain a Member-State review before setting the flow. I did not find a reliable current country-by-country matrix in the corpus.

7. **Check whether the DSA applies**
   - If the app qualifies as an **online platform accessible to minors**, additional protections apply. The Commission’s current guidance recommends private-by-default minor accounts, safer recommender systems, child-friendly controls, and proportionate age assurance: [Commission guidelines on protection of minors](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors).
   - Such platforms must also avoid profiling-based advertising to minors: [EDPB guidelines on the interplay between the DSA and GDPR](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2025/interplay-between-dsa-and-gdpr-edpb-adopts-guidelines_en).

**Before design sign-off, I would require:** a screen-by-screen data map, lawful-basis and SDK inventory, child-comprehension testing, consent/default-state review, age-assurance decision, and a DSA applicability check.

**EU launch checklist**

- **Use concise, plain, age-appropriate language.** Avoid vague labels such as “improve your experience.” Explain what data is used and the practical consequence—for example, “We use your location to show nearby events.” Information must be transparent, intelligible and easily accessible, especially for children: [EDPB transparency guidelines](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/transparency_en).
- **Use layered and contextual notices.** Put essential information in onboarding and immediately before permissions or new data uses, with the complete notice one tap away. Clearly identify each purpose and its lawful basis when data is obtained: [Facebook transparency decision](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2023-01/facebook-18-5-5_final_decision_redacted_en.pdf).
- **Make consent genuine where you rely on it.** Keep optional processing separate from service acceptance; use unticked, granular choices; and make refusal and later withdrawal straightforward. Do not bundle or pressure users: [EDPB consent guidelines](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-052020-consent-under-regulation-2016679_en).
- **Avoid manipulative UI.** No prominent “accept” paired with hidden refusal, repeated prompts, emotional pressure or confusing toggles. The EDPB has ordered removal of unfair consent designs: [TikTok unfair-design decision](https://edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2023/following-edpb-decision-tiktok-ordered-eliminate-unfair-design-practices-concerning_en).
- **Handle age appropriately.** Determine whether you need age assurance to apply child-specific settings or consent rules. If you use it, collect only what is necessary and choose a proportionate, privacy-preserving method—not an identity-document check by default: [BfDI age-verification requirements](https://www.bfdi.bund.de/DE/BfDI/Inhalte/Reden/2025/2025-09-01_Altersverifikationssysteme.html?nn=251864).
- **Design protection into the defaults.** Child privacy and safety should be addressed during product design, not left to disclosures alone: [G7 child-protection-by-design statement](https://www.bfdi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/2025/07_G7-Roundtable.html?nn=251944).

Before release, have privacy/legal map the flow against each EU country’s child-consent threshold and verify the complete GDPR Article 13/14 notice content. Also test comprehension with users in the youngest expected age group—not just with adults.

Yes. Under GDPR, privacy choices should shape the architecture—not be added after launch. Before freezing schemas, APIs, and defaults, address:

1. **Map every data flow and purpose**
   - Record what you collect, why, where it goes, who can access it, and the legal basis.
   - Avoid generic “future use” fields and separate data used for different purposes.

2. **Make the least-invasive configuration the default**
   - Collect only data necessary for the core feature.
   - Default optional analytics, profiling, sharing, discoverability, and extended retention to off.
   - Limit default accessibility and internal permissions. This follows the EDPB’s [Guidelines on Data Protection by Design and by Default](https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-42019-article-25-data-protection-design-and_en).

3. **Build retention and deletion into the data model**
   - Assign retention periods by data type.
   - Support automated deletion across primary stores, logs, caches, search indexes, backups, and downstream processors.
   - Preserve only what has a documented reason to remain.

4. **Design for user rights**
   - Make it technically feasible to locate, export, correct, restrict, object to processing of, and erase a person’s data.
   - Include identity verification and request tracking without creating unnecessary new data. The EDPB specifically expects technical solutions supporting objection and erasure: [One-Stop-Shop Case Digest](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/documents/support-pool-of-experts/one-stop-shop-case-digest-on-right-to-object-and-right-to-erasure_en).

5. **Run a DPIA screening now**
   - If the planned processing is likely to create high risks, the DPIA must be completed **before processing begins**, assessing necessity, proportionality, risks, and mitigations: [DPIA Guidelines](https://www.cnil.fr/sites/default/files/atoms/files/20171013_wp248_rev01_enpdf_4.pdf).
   - Repeat the assessment when purposes, scope, technology, or risk changes.

6. **Treat security as a processing-design issue**
   - Establish data classification, encryption, tenant isolation, least privilege, audit logging, secrets management, recovery, and breach detection.
   - Review measures periodically and after architectural changes: [When to review data-protection measures](https://www.aepd.es/en/prensa-y-comunicacion/blog/when-to-review-data-protection-measures).

7. **Keep production data out of development by default**
   - Prefer synthetic or properly anonymised test data.
   - If real data is genuinely necessary, document why and apply production-grade access controls: [Personal Data Breaches: Development and Pre-Production Environments](https://www.aepd.es/en/prensa-y-comunicacion/blog/data-breaches-development-and-pre-production-enviroments).

8. **Make vendors and hosting replaceable and auditable**
   - Inventory cloud providers, SDKs, analytics tools, subprocessors, and transfer locations.
   - Processor relationships require appropriate Article 28 contracts, careful selection, and monitoring: [Processor guidance](https://www.datenschutz-bayern.de/technik/orient/oh_auftragsverarbeitung.pdf).
   - Avoid designs that make deletion, regional processing, or changing a vendor impractical.

A useful engineering gate is: **no new data field, event, integration, or model input without a documented purpose, legal basis, retention rule, access policy, deletion path, and owner.**

Yes. Privacy needs to be an architectural constraint, not a pre-launch review. The [EDPB’s Article 25 guidelines](https://edpb.europa.eu/our-work-tools/our-documents/guidelines/guidelines-42019-article-25-data-protection-design-and_en) require appropriate technical and organisational measures **by design and by default**, considering state of the art and documenting their effectiveness.

Lock in these items now:

- **Data boundaries:** inventory each data field, its purpose and where it flows. Avoid collecting optional data by default.
- **Privacy-preserving defaults:** minimum visibility, sharing, telemetry and retention; optional tracking or personalisation should not start enabled.
- **Deletion and retention:** attach retention rules to datasets, backups, logs and derived data. Build account deletion and erasure workflows across all systems. CNIL’s recent enforcement found procedural gaps around erasure: [Right-to-erasure enforcement findings](https://www.cnil.fr/fr/droit-effacement-bilan-cnil-action-europeenne).
- **Rights support:** make access, correction, export and deletion technically feasible without manual database work.
- **Security and separation:** least-privilege access, encryption, tenant isolation, audit trails and separate production data from development/test environments.
- **Vendor lifecycle:** record which processors receive which data; ensure they follow instructions, secure it and delete it when the relationship ends. These remain active CNIL enforcement areas: [CNIL’s 2025 sanctions and corrective measures](https://www.cnil.fr/en/sanctions-and-corrective-measures-cnils-actions-2025).
- **Consent/tracker architecture:** keep non-essential trackers separable so the product works before consent and after refusal.
- **Risk assessment:** if processing is likely to be high risk, conduct a DPIA **before processing**, assessing necessity, proportionality and mitigations: [DPIA guidance](https://www.cnil.fr/sites/default/files/atoms/files/20171013_wp248_rev01_enpdf_4.pdf). The EDPB also released a [DPIA template](https://idpc.org.mt/news-latest/enhancing-compliance-and-consistency-edpb-adopts-dpia-template/) in April 2026.
- **Evidence:** retain design decisions, threat models, test results and measurable privacy controls. Article 25 expects effectiveness to be demonstrable.

Yes. The biggest redesign risk is blurring the line between insured deposits and third-party investments.

### Navigation and FDIC treatment

Under the [FDIC’s 2026 final rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-29/pdf/2026-01806.pdf), the app and website should:

- Display the official FDIC digital sign **clearly, continuously and conspicuously** on the initial/home screen, login screen and first screen of the deposit-account-opening flow.
- Show the non-deposit disclosure on screens primarily dedicated to investments: **not FDIC insured, not a deposit and may lose value**.
- Present a **once-per-session notification** when a logged-in customer crosses from the bank’s digital channel to the third party’s investment platform. It may be dismissed or disappear automatically after at least three seconds.
- Avoid navigation labels, shared product cards or visual treatment that could imply investments are bank deposits or bank-guaranteed. A disclaimer does not necessarily cure an otherwise misleading presentation, according to [CFPB guidance on deposit-insurance representations](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/circulars/circular-2022-02-deception-representations-involving-the-fdics-name-or-logo-or-deposit-insurance/).

The FDIC has also published [updated implementation Q&As](https://www.fdic.gov/news/financial-institution-letters/2026/updated-questions-and-answers-regarding-fdic-official-signs). Compliance should confirm the final implementation date; the corpus confirms an extension but does not provide the exact date.

### Account-opening flow

Build these into the screen requirements rather than treating them as post-design legal copy:

- **Accurate product economics:** Product names, APY/rates, fees, minimum-balance conditions and product differences must be consistent throughout marketing, comparison and opening screens. The CFPB has pursued misleading savings-account rate and product distinctions under TISA/Regulation DD and the CFPA—see [Capital One enforcement](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/enforcement/actions/capital-one-national-association-and-capital-one-financial-corporation/).
- **CIP/identity verification:** Collect the required identifying information before opening and support document or non-documentary verification and recordkeeping under [31 CFR §1020.220](http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CFR-2013-title31-vol3/pdf/CFR-2013-title31-vol3-sec1020-220.pdf). If information is prefilled, customers must be able to review, correct and confirm it, per [FDIC guidance](https://fdic.gov/news/financial-institution-letters/2025/fdic-supervisory-approach-regarding-use-pre-populated).
- **Overdraft choice:** If offered, obtain affirmative consent before charging overdraft fees on ATM and one-time debit-card transactions. Provide the notice before opt-in, retain evidence, send confirmation and permit revocation—see [CFPB Circular 2024-05](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/circulars/consumer-financial-protection-circular-2024-05/).
- **Privacy:** Deliver the applicable initial privacy notice and a genuine opt-out opportunity where required, consistent with the [FDIC Privacy Rule Handbook](https://www.fdic.gov/bank-examinations/privacy-rule-handbook).
- **Electronic authorizations and records:** Keep disclosures and authorizations accessible, reproducible and retained. Preauthorized EFTs require signed or similarly authenticated authorization and a copy for the customer, per the [CFPB’s EFT authorization bulletin](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/compliance/supervisory-guidance/bulletin-consumer-authorizations-preauthorized-eft/).

### Recommended release gates

Require Compliance approval of:

1. A screen-by-screen FDIC/non-deposit-signage map.
2. The deposit-to-investment transition behavior, including session logic and deep links.
3. Disclosure timing and E-SIGN delivery/consent.
4. All rate, fee and overdraft representations.
5. CIP, privacy and decline/error paths.
6. Mobile, web, responsive, screen-reader and third-party-webview testing.
7. Evidence retention showing which disclosure version each applicant saw and accepted.

State-law, account-type and investment-partner requirements may add further controls, so those should be reviewed once the proposed flow and target customer states are fixed.

The main issue is the **Data Protection Officer’s position**.

- **Do not end or effectively curtail the DPO’s current designation as part of the reorganisation without first obtaining the EDPS’s consent.** Since February 2026, prior EDPS consent is required before dismissing a DPO before the end of their term. Calling the change a restructuring would not safely avoid that requirement if its practical effect is to remove or replace the DPO. See [EDPS: new guidance and binding rules protecting DPO independence](https://www.edps.europa.eu/press-publications/press-news/press-releases/2026/edps-strengthens-dpo-role-new-guidance-and-binding-rules-protect-dpo-independence-across-eu-institutions_en).

See [EDPS Supervisory Guidance on the Role of DPOs in EU institutions](https://www.edps.europa.eu/data-protection/our-work/publications/guidelines/2025-12-18-edps-guidance-role-data-protection-officers-eu-institutions-bodies-offices-and-agencies_en).

Yes. Louisiana changed the limits effective **August 1, 2025**, so the prior product settings may be obsolete.

- **Size:** The amount paid to a borrower in a deferred-presentment transaction increased from **$350 to $700**. The framework also applies a maximum **aggregate outstanding principal balance** across covered deferred-presentment transactions and small loans.
- **Annual adjustment:** OFI must publish an inflation-adjusted maximum by **September 1 each year**, using CPI and rounding up to the nearest $10. For a cycle extending beyond September 1, the product limit should be configurable rather than hard-coded. See [Maximum Outstanding Principal Balance for Deferred Presentment Transactions and Small Loans](https://ofi.la.gov/maximum-outstanding-principal-balance-for-deferred-presentment-transactions-and-small-loans/).
- **Pricing:** Act 510 removed the former **$45 maximum fee/interest cap** for these products. That should not be interpreted as eliminating every applicable pricing or disclosure restriction; the fee methodology and product classification still need validation. See [2025 Deferred Presentment and Small Loan Legislation](https://ofi.la.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/NonDep_2025DeferredPresentmentAndSmallLoanLegislation_08012025.pdf).
- **Credit reporting:** Covered lenders may not report negative customer information to credit bureaus, which could affect underwriting and loss assumptions. See [Deferred Presentment and Small Loan Legislation—Effective August 1, 2025](https://ofi.la.gov/deferred-presentment-and-small-loan-legislation-effective-august-1-2025/).

**Recommended launch controls:** classify each redesigned loan to confirm whether it falls under this Act or the broader Louisiana consumer-credit regime; cap aggregate exposure at the then-current OFI amount; and recheck the OFI publication immediately before launch and again after September 1. The corpus did not surface enough current detail to validate the complete permissible pricing formula for any installment product outside this specific Act.

### Critical deadline: 30 June 2026

Italy’s latest position is that existing VASPs must **hold MiCAR CASP authorisation by 30 June 2026** to continue operating. Local VASP/OAM registration is not a substitute. See [CONSOB — Weekly newsletter No. 18, 11 May 2026](https://www.consob.it/web/consob-and-its-activities/-/weekly-newsletter-year-xxxii-no.-18-11-may-2026?redirect=%2Fweb%2Fconsob-and-its-activities%2Fnewsletter%2Flatests).

Because we currently have no MiCAR authorisation, continued custody and exchange services from **1 July** should not be included in the roadmap unless authorisation is obtained. ESMA expects unauthorised firms to cease services and have an executable, client-protective wind-down plan by then: [ESMA — Statement on the end of transitional periods under MiCA](https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2026-04/ESMA75-113276571-1679_Statement_on_the_end_of_transitional_periods_under_MiCA.pdf).

### Immediate actions

1. **Escalate to the board and regulatory counsel today.** Confirm whether any MiCAR application is pending and whether we are validly covered by Italy’s transition for the remaining two weeks. The available records do not establish that registration alone guarantees this.
2. **Run two tracks immediately:**
   - pursue/confirm authorisation with Banca d’Italia/CONSOB; and
   - prepare a 1 July wind-down or migration to an authorised CASP, covering client notices, withdrawals/transfers, custody release and contract termination.
3. **Do not plan new H2 launches or expansion on the current registration.** If authorisation will not be in hand, onboarding, marketing and ordinary service provision must stop, with activity limited to orderly exit.
4. **Audit every supported stablecoin now.** Services involving non-MiCA-compliant ARTs or EMTs should already have ceased, subject only to the expired transition arrangements: [ESMA — Non-MiCA-compliant ARTs and EMTs](https://www.esma.europa.eu/document/statement-provision-certain-crypto-asset-services-relation-non-mica-compliant-arts-and).
5. **Check the authorisation-readiness workstream:** governance and fitness, prudential safeguards, segregation/safekeeping of client assets, complaints, conflicts, outsourcing, business continuity/wind-down, DORA, AML/CFT and Travel Rule controls. The Travel Rule includes procedures for detecting and handling missing transfer information: [EBA Travel Rule Guidelines](http://www.hcmc.gr/aweb/files/laundering/files/Travel%20Rule%20Guidelines_EN.pdf).

**Bottom line:** without MiCAR authorisation by 30 June, the compliant H2 roadmap is an orderly exit or migration—not continued operation under the local registration.

## Bottom line

**No—we cannot plan to continue the existing service unchanged in H2 2026.** The Italian transitional regime ends on **30 June 2026**. Our local VASP registration is not a substitute for MiCA authorisation after that date.

CONSOB states that VASPs must obtain MiCA CASP authorisation by 30 June ([Weekly newsletter, 11 May 2026](https://www.consob.it/web/consob-and-its-activities/-/weekly-newsletter-year-xxxii-no-18-11-may-2026?redirect=%2Fweb%2Fconsob-and-its-activities%2Fnewsletter%2Flatests)). ESMA similarly describes the transition as running only until **1 July 2026 or an authorisation decision, whichever comes first** ([Spotlight on Markets, December 2024](https://www.esma.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2025-01/Newsletter_December_2024.pdf)).

Therefore, unless we are **actually authorised by 1 July**, the H2 roadmap should assume that normal custody and exchange operations must stop—not merely that an application needs to be filed.

## Immediate priorities

1. **Escalate the authorisation status today.** Confirm whether any MiCA application has been submitted and whether authorisation before 1 July is realistically available.
2. **Prepare an executable wind-down/transfer plan now:** stop new business and marketing by the deadline, notify clients, and provide for asset withdrawals or migration to an authorised CASP. Continuing ordinary custody or exchange without authorisation creates material enforcement risk; CONSOB is already blocking unauthorised crypto-service websites ([CONSOB newsletter, 4 May 2026](https://www.consob.it/web/consob-and-its-activities/-/weekly-newsletter-year-xxxii-no.-17-4-may-2026?redirect=%2Fweb%2Fconsob-and-its-activities%2Fnewsletter%2Flatests)).
3. **If pursuing authorisation, fund a full MiCA remediation programme:** governance, prudential resources, client-asset safeguarding, conduct disclosures, complaints, conflicts, outsourcing, AML/CFT and orderly wind-down controls ([Banca d’Italia MiCAR communication](https://www.bancaditalia.it/media/approfondimenti/2024/micar/index.html)).
4. **Review every stablecoin.** Services involving non-MiCA-compliant stablecoins should not continue. For electronic-money-token activities that also constitute payment services, the EBA says firms needed PSD2 authorisation or an authorised PSP partner after **2 March 2026**; pending applicants face restrictions including no new clients or marketing ([EBA opinion, 12 February 2026](https://eba.europa.eu/publications-and-media/press-releases/eba-advises-national-authorities-actions-take-end-transition-period-under-its-no-action-letter)).
5. **Add the staff-competence deadline to H2:** CONSOB adopted ESMA’s MiCA knowledge-and-competence guidelines, effective six months after 28 January 2026—i.e. **28 July 2026** ([CONSOB newsletter, 30 March 2026](https://www.consob.it/web/consob-and-its-activities/-/weekly-newsletter-year-xxxii-no-12-30-march-2026?redirect=%2Fweb%2Fconsob-and-its-activities%2Fnewsletter)).

**Roadmap assumption:** no ordinary service from **1 July 2026** unless MiCA authorisation is in hand; otherwise H2 begins with controlled exit or migration to an authorised provider.

Yes. For **Q3 2026**, the main actions for continued IVD sales in the **EU/EEA and Switzerland** are:

### Immediate priorities

1. **Complete the EUDAMED transition**
   - Since **28 May 2026**, manufacturers, EU authorised representatives and importers must be registered in the Actor module.
   - Any device first placed on the EU market after that date must be registered in the UDI/Devices module **before placement**.
   - Devices already on the market before 28 May must be migrated by **27 November 2026**. Verify SRNs, actor data, Basic UDI-DIs, certificates and device records now.  
   [EUDAMED obligations from 28 May 2026](https://www.fagg.be/nl/news/eudamed_verduidelijkingen_over_de_verplichtingen_vanaf_28_mei_2026)

2. **Close the Class C legacy-device deadline**
   - For any Class C IVD relying on IVDR transitional provisions, confirm that a formal notified-body application was lodged by **26 May 2026**.
   - The written conformity-assessment agreement must be concluded by **26 September 2026** to retain the transition through **31 December 2028**.
   - If the May application deadline was missed, escalate immediately: the device does not qualify for that extension and would need full IVDR conformity before further placement.  
   [Fimea—Class C transition requirements](https://fimea.fi/-/in-vitro-diagnostiikan-laitevalmistaja-varmista-siirtymaaikojen-jatkon-edellytykset)

3. **Start Swiss device registration on 1 July**
   - From **1 July 2026**, IVD registration moves to the swissdamed UDI Devices module.
   - Coordinate with the Swiss authorised representative to register applicable products and sales units, with the portfolio transition ending **31 December 2026**.
   - New products should be registered before first Swiss placement. Registration becomes immediate where a product is involved in a serious incident, FSCA or trend report. Also verify that the representative’s CHRN and economic-operator data are current.  
   [Swissmedic—swissdamed registration requirement](https://www.swissmedic.ch/swissmedic/de/home/news/mitteilungen/swissdamed-registrierungspflicht.html)

### Add to the quarterly control cycle

- Confirm legacy products still have no significant design or intended-purpose changes and remain covered by the IVDR QMS and notified-body arrangements.
- Review planned discontinuations or supply interruptions. Where loss of availability could cause serious harm or public-health risk, the manufacturer must normally notify the competent authority and directly supplied parties **at least six months in advance**; downstream operators must cascade the notice.  
  [European Commission—Article 10a supply-interruption guidance](https://health.ec.europa.eu/document/download/b431b10f-8512-4f47-9191-e1b84b2f9a27_en?filename=mdr_qna-article10a_mdr-ivdr_en.pdf)
- Reconfirm PMS/vigilance responsibilities, importer details, storage/transport controls and Swiss representative labelling.

This assessment covers the **EU/EEA and Switzerland**. The UK, Türkiye and other non-EU European jurisdictions have separate requirements and would need the actual market list checked individually.

For any Class C legacy IVD relying on the extended IVDR transition:

- Verify that a formal conformity-assessment application was lodged with a notified body by **26 May 2026**.
- Conclude the written agreement with that notified body by **26 September 2026**.
- Confirm the other transition conditions remain satisfied, including the IVDR-compliant QMS and no significant design or intended-purpose changes.

Meeting these conditions allows eligible Class C devices to use the transition through **31 December 2028**. Swiss IVD product registration in the swissdamed UDI/Devices module becomes mandatory from **1 July 2026**, replacing the prior notification route for most IVDs.

- Align with the CH authorised representative on who will enter and maintain each device record.
- Prepare Swiss device, UDI, certificate and CH-REP data now.
- Use the transition period through **31 December 2026** to complete the existing portfolio.
- Keep the separate notification process in mind for repackaged/relabelled and in-house IVDs where applicable.

Source: [Swissmedic—Notification of IVDs](https://www.swissmedic.ch/swissmedic/en/home/medical-devices/market-access/meldung-ivd.html).

### 4. Keep ongoing controls active
- Maintain vigilance and serious-incident reporting to the relevant authorities, including Swissmedic.
- Review whether any planned supply interruption could trigger the EU’s advance-notification requirement—generally at least six months beforehand for affected devices presenting serious patient or public-health risk.
- Confirm Swiss importers are performing conformity checks, applying importer identification and observing storage/transport requirements; these were recent Swissmedic inspection findings. This covers the EU/EEA and Switzerland. A country list would be needed to identify any remaining national requirements or non-EU markets such as the UK.

Yes. Given that minors use the service and it combines social chat with AI companions, I would treat the following as release blockers.

### Build before launch

1. **Reliable age assurance and age-based feature controls**
   - Do not rely only on a date-of-birth declaration.
   - Support age bands and jurisdiction-specific rules, while minimising retained identity data.
   - The UK regulators expect effective, proportionate age assurance; platforms must also enforce any minimum age they advertise ([Joint ICO/Ofcom statement on age assurance](https://ico.org.uk/about-the-ico/media-centre/news-and-blogs/2026/03/joint-statement-from-ico-and-ofcom-on-age-assurance/)).
   - EU platforms accessible to minors need proportionate, privacy-preserving age assurance ([DSA minors guidelines](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-presents-guidelines-and-age-verification-app-prototype-safer-online-space-children)).
   - California’s proposed SB 976 regulations also contemplate age assurance and parental-consent processes; details are not final, so build a configurable flow ([California DOJ proposed SB 976 regulations](https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/california-department-justice-releases-proposed-protecting-our-kids-social-media)).

2. **Minor-safe defaults for social features**
   - Private profiles/accounts by default.
   - Block, mute and child-friendly report controls.
   - Consent before adding minors to groups.
   - Prevent discovery or unsolicited contact that creates grooming risk.
   - Tune recommenders away from harmful material and use explicit user choices rather than inferred engagement for minors. These are the Commission’s benchmarks for DSA Article 28 compliance ([Commission guidelines on protection of minors](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-publishes-guidelines-protection-minors)).

3. **Child-specific AI-companion guardrails**
   - Clearly and repeatedly identify companions as AI—not human.
   - Prevent sexual or romantic role-play involving minors, grooming behaviour, and encouragement of self-harm or dangerous conduct.
   - Add crisis detection with safe responses and routes to human/emergency support.
   - Include reporting, moderation logging and rapid model/character disablement.
   - EU chatbot disclosure obligations apply from **2 August 2026**, so this release should include the disclosure layer ([Chatbot transparency and AI Act timing](https://www.autoriteitpersoonsgegevens.nl/en/current/ap-and-acm-chatbots-should-not-fully-replace-humans-in-customer-service)).
   - US state attorneys general have specifically demanded guardrails preventing AI systems from sexualising children ([AG coalition warning](https://www.iowaattorneygeneral.gov/newsroom/attorney-general-brenna-bird-demands-companies-end-predatory-ai-interactions-with-kids/)).

4. **Privacy and consent controls**
   - Child-readable privacy notices in English and Italian.
   - Explicit explanation of whether chats are used for model training.
   - A working opt-out from training and deletion/access/objection flows.
   - Parental-consent support where consent is the lawful basis—for example, the UK requires it for under-13s ([ICO statement](https://ico.org.uk/about-the-ico/media-centre/news-and-blogs/2026/06/ico-statement-on-uk-government-announcement-about-social-media-restrictions-for-under-16s/)).
   - No profiling-based targeted ads to known minors in Italy/EU ([Two years of the DSA](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/two-years-digital-services-act-allows-50-million-content-moderation-decisions-platforms-be-reversed)).
   - Italy’s regulator has already required AI services to provide transparent data-use information, training opt-outs and effective age controls ([Garante/OpenAI measures](https://www.garanteprivacy.it/garante/doc.jsp?ID=9882865)).

5. **Moderation and appeals**
   - In-app reporting for harmful users, content and AI responses.
   - Operational removal/escalation queues and enforcement against repeat offenders.
   - Notify users of moderation decisions and provide an appeal path for EU users, as required under the DSA ([DSA appeal requirements](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/two-years-digital-services-act-allows-50-million-content-moderation-decisions-platforms-be-reversed)).

### Non-code launch gates

Complete and approve a child-safety risk assessment and DPIA covering social interaction, recommenders, AI conversations, profiling, sensitive disclosures and age assurance. California privacy risk-assessment rules have applied since **1 January 2026** where the business and processing fall within scope ([California privacy regulations](https://cppa.ca.gov/announcements/2025/20250923.html)).

I would **not ship** if the release still has DOB-only age gating, public-by-default minor accounts, unrestricted minor AI role-play, no training opt-out, or no reporting/appeal workflow. The announced UK under-16 social-media restriction is still a policy proposal, so it does not by itself require a blanket UK 16+ gate today.

### P0 before shipping

   - Enforce your stated minimum age and support at least under-13, 13–15, and 16+ handling.

   - In the US, collecting known under-13 users’ information without verifiable parental consent creates COPPA exposure: [FTC Sendit enforcement](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/09/ftc-alleges-sendit-app-its-ceo-unlawfully-collected-personal-data-children-deceived-users-about).

   - Provide an easy illegal-content reporting flow, moderation decisions with reasons, and an appeal mechanism.

   - Include in-product reporting for cyberbullying, sexual exploitation and non-consensual intimate content, with a priority moderation queue and the ability to execute regulator removal orders promptly.

5. **Release evidence**
   - Record how the new feature affects minors, age assurance, profiling, AI training, retention and foreseeable harms.
   - Keep test evidence showing that minors cannot bypass restricted experiences and that reporting, deletion and escalation flows work. UK regulators expect platforms to demonstrate their age-assurance compliance: [ICO open letter](https://ico.org.uk/about-the-ico/media-centre/news-and-blogs/2026/03/open-letter-issued-to-tech-firms-to-strengthen-age-checks-and-protect-children-s-data/).

California has proposed SB 976 regulations covering age assurance and parental-consent processes, but the record I found describes them as **proposed**, so I would architect for them now rather than represent the proposal itself as a final release requirement: [California DOJ proposed SB 976 regulations](https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/california-department-justice-releases-proposed-protecting-our-kids-social-media).
